summary: This paper introduces an efficient protocol for learning single-qubit mid-circuit measurement (MCM) instruments on superconducting qubits by measuring readout-backaction correlations from three repeated MCMs on a maximally mixed input. The learned instrument, which is $Z$-twirled to eliminate coherences while preserving joint classical-outcome and post-measurement-state statistics, improves Pauli-observable prediction by $\sim 100\times$ over confusion-matrix models on IBM Heron transmons and reveals $T_1$-decay-dominated backaction with $\eta_{\downarrow} \gg \eta_{\uparrow}$ ($10^1$--$10^2$ asymmetry).
motivation: Conventional confusion-matrix characterization of terminal measurements is insufficient for dynamic circuits because mid-circuit measurements both produce classical readout and alter the quantum state; accurately modeling these readout-backaction correlations and excitation-decay asymmetry is essential for syndrome extraction, reset, and SPAM error separation.
method: The protocol applies $Z$-twirling to reduce the MCM to a pair of 2×2 conditional-probability matrices $M^{(0)}, M^{(1)}$ mapping pre-measurement basis states and classical outcomes to post-measurement basis states; repeated MCM chains of length $L=3$ on maximally mixed input via Pauli randomization yield all five gauge-invariant scalars (one single-shot probability plus traces and determinants) via closed-form Cayley-Hamilton recurrence relations, leaving only one unidentifiable gauge parameter $t$ that is tightly constrained by physicality ($0 \le M_{s',s}^{(o)}(t) \le 1$).
result: On 60 qubits across three IBM Heron devices (ibm_kingston, ibm_pittsburgh, ibm_boston), the learned instrument predicts depth-10 $X$-interleaved validation circuits with absolute $\langle Z \rangle$ deviations $\lesssim 10^{-3}$ versus $10^{-2}$ for confusion-matrix models; gauge bands are typically $<10\%$ relative width due to tight physicality constraints; self-consistency checks via Cayley-Hamilton recurrences show no statistically resolved violations of stationarity or Markovianity.
